title: "Series base templates: tflspec_summary and tflspec_hierarchy"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
knitr::opts_template$set(code = list(comment = "", class.output = "r"))
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")
```

A report does not have to be written from nothing. It can name a
**series base template** and write only what differs. This article shows
what such a template is, the two base templates of the `tflspec_v1`
series, `tflspec_summary` and `tflspec_hierarchy`, and the series values
a study can change. A last section is for the people who write
templates. The data is the package's fictional example data (`adsl`,
`adae`).

## What a series base template is

A series is a folder of templates with a version in its name. tflspec
comes with one, `tflspec_v1`. Each template is one YAML file under
`inst/series/tflspec_v1/templates/`.

A base template holds two things:

- **the processing definition**: the data rows, the analysis items, and
  the content (the rtfreporter plan) of one kind of table;
- **a full set of defaults**: a value for each argument that does not
  have to come from the report.

A report names the template under `template:` and gives its arguments
under `args:`:

```yaml
template:
  name: tflspec_v1/tflspec_summary
  args:
    by: [TRT01A]
    continuous: [AGE]
```

The template fills its `"{name}"` spots with these values. Where the
report gives no value, the template's default applies. The result is an
ordinary report SPEC.

A report changes the table in two ways:

- **by an argument**: `args:` gives a value in place of the default. A
  map whose default is a series value (`formats`) is the exception: the
  report's names go over the series' map one by one, a name whose value
  is `!unset` is removed (for `formats`, that statistic then takes the
  ARD catalog's format), and the names the report does not write keep
  the series' values (see [Series values](#series-values));
- **by an appended card**: the report's own `content:` lists plan items
  (cards) that come after the template's. When the template already has
  a card of the same verb, the two become one. The last one wins, and
  only the arguments the report writes change; the template's other
  arguments stay. (A few verbs that stack, such as `plan_filter`, add a
  card instead.)

The arguments of a template, with their defaults, are listed by
`tfl_arg_defs()`:

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(tflspec)

defs <- tfl_arg_defs(template = "tflspec_v1/tflspec_summary")
defs[, c("name", "step", "required")]
```

## A study to work in

The examples run in one small study. `tfl_ai_study_init()` writes its
`study.yml`, `spec/data.yml` (the datasets and the analysis sets) and
`spec/defaults.yml`.

```{r, message = FALSE}
study <- file.path(tempdir(), "series-study")
dir.create(file.path(study, "adam"), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
for (x in c("adsl", "adae")) {
  saveRDS(get(x), file.path(study, "adam", paste0(x, ".rds")))
}
invisible(tfl_ai_study_init(study, adam = "adam", study_id = "SERIES-1"))
outputs <- file.path(study, "spec", "outputs")
```

A study reads its own copy of a series and of each template its reports
use, never the series's folder. `tfl_copy_templates()` copies them,
whole, into `spec/series/tflspec_v1/`, and writes there which file came
from where, when, and its md5 (`copied.yml`):

```{r}
copied <- tfl_copy_templates(study, c("tflspec_v1/tflspec_summary",
                                      "tflspec_v1/tflspec_hierarchy"))
copied[, c("template", "status")]
```

With no templates named, it copies every template the study's report
SPECs name that it has not copied yet. A study that needs a template of
its own copies one under a new name (`as = "summary_wide"`), then edits
the copy.

One helper does the same steps for each report. It fills the template in
(`tfl_template_resolve()`), saves the report in the study, and returns
the report, its ARD program (`tfl_ard_code()`), its ARD
(`tfl_build_ard()`) and its table program (`tfl_content_code()`).

```{r}
run_report <- function(file) {
  out <- tfl_template_resolve(file, study = file.path(study, "study.yml"))
  tfl_write_output(out, file.path(outputs, basename(file)))
  st <- tfl_read_study_spec(study)
  out <- tfl_read_output(file.path(outputs, basename(file)))
  list(spec = out, study = st,
       ard_code = tfl_ard_code(st, output_id = out$id, save = FALSE, part = "body"),
       ard = suppressMessages(tfl_build_ard(st, dir = study, output_id = out$id, save = FALSE)),
       table_code = tfl_content_code(out, study = st))
}
```

## `tflspec_summary`

### What it is for

`tflspec_summary` makes a summary table of one row per subject: the
descriptive statistics of continuous variables and the counts of
categorical variables, one column a group. Demographics and baseline
characteristics are the usual uses. It reads the ADSL-like data of one
analysis set.

### Its arguments

- `by` is required: the column variable(s), the groups across.
- `continuous` and `categorical`: the variables, in the order of the
  rows. Give at least one of them. Neither has a default: the template
  holds no set of variables of its own.
- `population`: the analysis set. Its default is
  `!series population_safety`, the series value (`SAF`, see below).
- `total`, `missing_row`, `formats`, `cells`, `count_cell`, `labels`,
  `max_rows` ... change the look of the table.

The page header prints the analysis set's label through the token
`{OUTPUT_POPULATION}`. A template report has no `common: population`, so
the label comes from the set its `adsl_sub` row keeps (its label in
`spec/data.yml`).

Three params change the content:

- `value_labels`: the label of each value of a variable, code to text
  (`{SEX: {F: Female, M: Male}}`). Empty: the code list's labels.
- `nest`: a variable's rows under one level of another,
  `{nested variable: {parent variable: level}}`. Write the level as the
  table shows it.
- `col_header`: the column header lines, each a map of cell texts.
  Empty (the default): the study's defaults apply, the column header of
  its `spec/defaults.yml`.

### Example: a demographics table

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = file.path(tempdir(), "T-DM.yml"), lang = "yaml")}
id: T-DM
kind: table
label: Demographic characteristics
template:
  name: tflspec_v1/tflspec_summary
  args:
    by: [TRT01A]
    continuous: [AGE]
    categorical: [SEX, RACE]
    labels: {AGE: "Age (years)", SEX: Sex, RACE: Race}
    value_labels: {SEX: {F: Female, M: Male}}
```

```{r}
dm <- run_report(file.path(tempdir(), "T-DM.yml"))
```

The data rows and the analyses of the ARD program:

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
cat(dm$ard_code, sep = "\n")
```

The analyses it makes, one a variable, and `BIGN` (the subjects of each
column):

```{r}
unique(dm$ard$analysis_id)
```

The table program:

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
cat(dm$table_code, sep = "\n")
```

The analysis set is `SAF`, so `{OUTPUT_POPULATION}` prints its label:

```{r}
tfl_report_tokens(dm$spec, study = dm$study)[["OUTPUT_POPULATION"]]
```

The report program puts the token in the page header, on its own line:

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
cat(tfl_report_code(dm$spec, content = "plan", study = dm$study), sep = "\n")
```

### Example: an appended card

The template pages the table at `max_rows` rows, and says how a page
splits (`split: group_safe`). Here the report appends a
`plan_paginate_rows` card that writes only `max_rows`:

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = file.path(tempdir(), "T-DM2.yml"), lang = "yaml")}
id: T-DM2
kind: table
label: Demographic characteristics, shorter pages
template:
  name: tflspec_v1/tflspec_summary
  args:
    by: [TRT01A]
    continuous: [AGE]
    categorical: [SEX, RACE]
content:
  - plan_paginate_rows: {max_rows: 20}
```

The two cards become one. The report's `max_rows` wins; the template's
`split` stays:

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
dm2 <- run_report(file.path(tempdir(), "T-DM2.yml"))
cat(tail(dm2$table_code, 1), sep = "\n")
```

For a single value such as `max_rows`, the argument is the simpler way.
A card is for what the template has no argument for.

## `tflspec_hierarchy`

### What it is for

`tflspec_hierarchy` counts the records of a dataset in a hierarchy,
outer level first: a system organ class, then a preferred term; a
medication class, then a name. Each row has the number and percentage of
subjects of each group. It is not tied to one dataset.

### Its arguments

- `from` is required: the dataset of the records (`ADAE`).
- `hierarchy` is required: the levels of the rows, outer first.
- `by` is required: the column variable(s).
- `any_row` (default `true`): a first row of the subjects with at least
  one record. `any_row_label` is its text.
- `sort_column`: the group whose count orders the rows, the most
  frequent first. Empty (the default): the total of all columns. For a
  finer order, append a `plan_sort` card.
- `min_pct`: keep only the rows with at least this percentage (`0` keeps
  every row). `min_pct_in` says where it must be reached: `any` group,
  `all` groups, or the `total` column (this needs `total: true`).
- `empty_text`: the sentence printed when no record is left. Empty: no
  sentence.

The records to count are not an argument. They are the report's own
`where:` on the template's `rec_sub` data row.

The analyses are one a depth: `ANY` (the any row), `L1` (the outer
level), `L2` (the next level), and so on. `analysis_ids` renames them,
keyed by depth (`{ANY: AEANY, L2: AEPT}`).

### Example: TEAEs by SOC and PT

```{cat, engine.opts = list(file = file.path(tempdir(), "T-AE.yml"), lang = "yaml")}
id: T-AE
kind: table
label: Treatment-emergent adverse events by SOC and PT
data:
  - id: rec_sub
    where: !r TRTEMFL == "Y"
template:
  name: tflspec_v1/tflspec_hierarchy
  args:
    from: ADAE
    by: [TRT01A]
    hierarchy: [AEBODSYS, AEDECOD]
```

```{r}
ae <- run_report(file.path(tempdir(), "T-AE.yml"))
```

The data rows: the report's `where:` is on `rec_sub`, merged into the
template's row.

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
cat(ae$ard_code, sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
unique(ae$ard$analysis_id)
```

The table program. Its `plan_sort` comes from `sort_column` (empty: the
total of all columns):

```{r, opts.label = "code"}
cat(ae$table_code, sep = "\n")
```

## Series values

Some defaults are not written in the template. They are written
`!series K`, and read from the series's common file,
`series.yml`, under `values:`:

```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(system.file("series", "tflspec_v1", "series.yml", package = "tflspec")),
    sep = "\n")
```

A template may read the study before the series. The two listing
templates write their style as

```yaml
style: !study {key: settings.style, fallback: !series style_listing}
```

so a listing's style is the study's `settings.style` (`study.yml`),
and the series's `style_listing` (`tfl_small` above) only when the
study has none. The header and the footnotes of the study's style reach
the listings too. A series's `values:` hold no `!study`: the series is
the study's fallback.

A study changes them in its own copy of `series.yml`
(`spec/series/tflspec_v1/series.yml`), under `values:`. It may edit the
file, or let `tfl_series_values_set()` write the values (the rest of the
file stays as it is):

```{r}
tfl_series_values_set(study, "tflspec_v1",
                      list(any_row_label = "Subjects with at least one TEAE"))
f <- file.path(study, "spec", "series", "tflspec_v1", "series.yml")
yaml::read_yaml(f)$values$any_row_label
```

The AE report now prints the study's text in its first row, with no
change to the report:

```{r}
ae2 <- run_report(file.path(tempdir(), "T-AE.yml"))
na <- Filter(function(i) i$fn == "normalize_ard", ae2$spec$content)
na[[1]]$args$overall
```

A report that writes a map argument whose default is `!series K`
changes only the names it writes. With the series's `formats` above,

```yaml
template:
  name: tflspec_v1/tflspec_summary
  analysis:
    formats: {mean: 3, "AGE:sd": !unset}
```

gives `mean` 3 decimals, drops `AGE:sd`, and keeps `N`, `sd`, `median`
and the others as the series has them. A map inside the map (one
variable's statistics) is put over in the same way. Other arguments, a
list such as `hierarchy` among them, are replaced whole.

## For template authors: `derive:`

A template may need a value that is worked out from its arguments: the
last level of a hierarchy, or a card's arguments only when a flag is on.
The template's `derive:` map gives such values names of their own. Each
name is one operation. The names are worked out in the order written,
once the arguments are known, and the template's sections use them as
`"{name}"`.

The operations:

| Operation | Gives |
|---|---|
| `value: x` | `x` as it is filled in |
| `if: x, then: a, else: b` | `a` when `x` is something (not empty, `false` or `""`), else `b` (default nothing) |
| `last: x` | the last element of the list `x` |
| `but_last: x` | all but the last (nothing for fewer than two) |
| `join: x, sep: s` | the elements as one text, `s` between them (default `", "`) |
| `keys: x, prefix: p` | a map `p1: x1, p2: x2, ...` |

Each gives nothing for an empty `x`. A value that is nothing drops its
key. A content item left with no arguments is dropped, so a step goes
away when its arguments derive to nothing.

A derived name is not an argument. A report cannot give it, it is not
in `tfl_arg_defs()`, and it cannot take a param's name.

Here is the `derive:` of `tflspec_hierarchy`:

```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
x <- readLines(system.file("series", "tflspec_v1", "templates", "tflspec_hierarchy.yml",
                           package = "tflspec"))
from <- grep("^derive:", x)
to <- grep("^data:", x) - 1L
cat(x[from:to], sep = "\n")
```

`hierarchy_total` is a map only when `total` is on, so with `total:
false` the template's `plan_total: "{hierarchy_total}"` is left out.
`hierarchy_empty` does the same for `plan_empty` when `empty_text` is
empty. The TEAE table above has no Total column, so it has no
`plan_total`:

```{r}
vapply(ae$spec$content, function(i) i$fn, "")
```
